Cursory means done quickly and without proper care or attention. When something is done in a cursory way, it is shallow and rushed — just enough to say it was done, but not enough to actually do it well.

Think of it like this: imagine you're supposed to read a 10-page report before a meeting. But instead of actually reading it, you just flip through the pages quickly, glancing at a few words here and there, and call it done. That's a cursory read. You technically "read" it, but not really.
The Feeling the Word Carries

Cursory almost always carries a mildly negative or critical tone. When you call something cursory, you are saying — either directly or between the lines — that it was not good enough. That more care, more time, or more attention was needed, but wasn't given.

It's the difference between a glance and a gaze. Between skimming and studying. Between going through the motions and actually trying.
The Two Ideas Packed Into This One Word

Cursory combines two things at once:

Speed — it was done too quickly.
Shallowness — it didn't go deep enough.

Both ideas live inside this word together. Something cursory is always both fast and superficial. That's what makes it different from a word like "brief," which just means short, without any judgment about quality.
Where You'll Commonly See It Used

Cursory almost always appears before a noun. The most natural pairings you'll see are:

  • a cursory glance (looked at it briefly, without really seeing it)
  • a cursory look (similar — a quick, uncommitted look)
  • a cursory inspection (checked it, but not carefully)
  • a cursory examination (went over it, but too shallowly)
  • a cursory review (reviewed it, but only at the surface)
  • a cursory reading (read it, but without real engagement)

You can also hear things like a cursory apology, a cursory nod, or a cursory mention — all carrying that same flavour of something done with minimal effort or sincerity.
Example Sentences

These will show you the word in action across different situations:

  • "The doctor gave the patient only a cursory examination before writing a prescription." (Meaning: the check-up was too quick and not thorough enough — potentially dangerous.)
  • "She gave the contract a cursory read and signed it without noticing the hidden fees." (Meaning: she didn't read it carefully, and that cost her.)
  • "The security guard did a cursory check of the bags and waved everyone through." (Meaning: he checked the bags, but so quickly that he wouldn't have found anything suspicious.)
  • "Even a cursory glance at the data shows that something is clearly wrong." (Meaning: you don't even need to look hard — it's obvious at first sight. This is a slightly different use, where cursory means "even the most basic or minimal look.")
  • "He offered a cursory apology and walked away." (Meaning: the apology was hollow — short, careless, insincere.)
A Note on That Last Example

The fourth sentence above shows you an interesting twist. Sometimes "cursory" is used to actually downplay how much effort something needs — as in, "you don't even need to try hard to see this." This use is less common but worth knowing. Context will always make the meaning clear.
Words That Mean Something Similar

These words are close to cursory, but each has its own slight difference:

  • Hasty — focused mostly on speed ("a hasty decision")
  • Superficial — focused mostly on lack of depth ("a superficial understanding")
  • Perfunctory — done as a formality, with no genuine effort or feeling ("a perfunctory greeting"); this is the closest word to cursory in both meaning and tone
  • Shallow — lacking depth, but broader in use

None of these perfectly replace "cursory," which specifically suggests both quickness and shallowness together, often in the context of a task or examination of something.
Words That Mean the Opposite

• thorough
  • careful
  • meticulous
  • detailed
  • exhaustive
  • rigorous

If someone gives something a thorough review, they've done the opposite of a cursory one.
How Formal Is This Word?

Cursory is a moderately formal word. You'll see it often in writing — journalism, academic work, professional reports — but it's also perfectly natural in educated conversation. It's not so fancy that it sounds odd when spoken, but it's not everyday casual language either.
The One-Sentence Summary
Cursory describes something done too quickly and without enough care or attention — technically done, but not really.
KUR-suh-ree
